name: Bolivia
summary_text: Bolivia is workable for trans visitors — one of Latin America's legal pioneers on paper. The 2016 Gender Identity Law was ground-breaking: legal gender recognition on the basis of self-declared identity (administrative process, no surgery), and gender identity is an explicitly protected ground in anti-discrimination law. Bolivia's constitution also names gender identity. Implementation lags the statute: the first national LGBTQ+ survey (2024) reveals significant exclusion in health, education, employment, and housing; social conservatism is strong outside La Paz/Santa Cruz; and bureaucrats often resist applying the Gender Identity Law. There is no documented pattern of police targeting of trans people as such, and no traveler-facing restriction — but also limited effective protection outside major cities.

sources.claim_summary: Comparative Politics article (April 2024) 'Activists, Parties, and the Expansion of Trans Rights in Bolivia': Bolivia prohibits gender-identity discrimination and passed a ground-breaking gender identity law (2016, allowing name/marker change) despite low voter support; trans activists leveraged access to ruling-party legislators; contradictory heteronormative laws passed alongside because both organised religion and LGBT activists were party constituents.

NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (WordPress critical error); the underlying Agencia Presentes article (Dec 2024) covers Bolivia's first virtual survey revealing the great exclusion of LGBTI people.

US State Department 2011 Human Rights Report for Bolivia: general human-rights assessment (arbitrary deprivation of life, prison conditions, corruption) - the LGBT section documents the constitutional anti-discrimination guarantee and societal discrimination.

sources.title: Trump’s Transgender Military Ban Leaves Only 18 Countries With Full LGBT Rights in Armed Forces - Newsweek
sources.claim_summary: Newsweek (July 2017): Trump's transgender military ban leaves the US off a short list of countries that do not legally discriminate on gender identity in the armed forces - comparative context including Bolivia's military policy.

sources.title: GFMER Sexual and Reproductive Rights Country Information - Bolivia - Jimena Villar de Onis
sources.claim_summary: Geneva Foundation for Medical Education and Research, Bolivia sexual and reproductive rights page: the Constitution prohibits discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity (Article 14(II)) and guarantees sexual rights (Article 66); documents the legal framework including abortion law.

sources.title: Militares gay, entre la discriminación y la clandestinidad en FFAA de Bolivia – eju.tv
sources.claim_summary: eju.tv/La Razón (Aug 2014, in Spanish): gay military personnel in Bolivia's armed forces live between discrimination and clandestinity - a soldier's hidden relationship with a captain; the TLGB collective and human-rights defenders call for openness in the institution.
